listeningParts.title: Volunteering on a wildlife survey
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a conservation charity to sign up for a weekend bird survey.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Hello, Westmoor Wildlife Trust, Karen speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I read in the local paper that you're looking for volunteers for a bird survey, and I'd like to find out more.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Oh, wonderful. Yes, we're doing our annual count of breeding birds on the Westmoor wetlands. We use the information to see how populations are changing from year to year. Have you done any bird surveys before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Not formally. I've been watching birds as a hobby for about five years, so I can recognise most of the common species, but I've never taken part in a proper survey.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: That's absolutely fine. Most of our volunteers start that way. Each new volunteer is paired with an experienced surveyor for the first day, so you'll learn the method as you go.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. When does the survey take place?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: We do two visits: one in April and one in June. The April visit is on the weekend of the twelfth and thirteenth. You'd only need to come on one of the days, though, not both.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I could do the Sunday. Saturdays are difficult for me.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Sunday the thirteenth, then. I should warn you, it's an early start. Birds are most active just after sunrise, so we meet at five forty-five in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wow, that is early. Where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: At the car park next to the visitor centre. Don't go to the main entrance on the road, because the gates aren't opened until nine. There's a separate track to the car park from Mill Lane. Look for the sign with a heron on it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Mill Lane, sign with a heron. Got it. How long does the survey last?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Usually about four hours. Each pair walks a fixed route, which we call a transect, and records every bird they see or hear within fifty metres of the path. You'll be back by about ten, and we provide breakfast at the visitor centre afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Breakfast sounds good after that. What do I need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Binoculars are the most important thing. If you don't have any, we can lend you a pair, but let me know in advance because we only have six. Bring waterproofs, even if the forecast is good, because the wetlands can be very wet underfoot, and wellington boots are better than walking boots.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I have binoculars, so that's fine. Do I need a notebook?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No, we'll give you a recording sheet and a clipboard. Some volunteers like to use an app on their phone instead, but we ask everyone to fill in the paper sheet as well, in case the phone battery runs out.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Makes sense. Is there any cost involved?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: No, volunteering is completely free. And all our volunteers get free entry to our nature reserves for the year. If you'd like to become a member of the Trust as well, that's twenty-four pounds a year, but there's no obligation at all.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very generous. Can I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Marcus Delaney. That's D-E-L-A-N-E-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know, any health issues for example?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm fine, but I'm allergic to bee stings. I carry medication with me.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me. I'll let your survey partner know. And one last thing: there's a short online training video about identifying birds by their songs. It's only twenty minutes, and it's really worth watching before the day, because about half of what you record will be birds you hear rather than see.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll definitely watch it tonight. Will I get the results of the survey afterwards?

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Yes, we send all volunteers a short report in the autumn, showing how the numbers compare with previous years. Last year, for example, we recorded our first pair of breeding bitterns for twenty years, which was very exciting.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's great. Thanks, Karen.

listeningParts.title: Rewilding at Hartwell Estate
listeningParts.contextDescription: The manager of a former farm explains a rewilding project to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, and welcome to Hartwell. My name is Tom Ashby, and my family farmed this land for four generations. Fifteen years ago, we made the decision to stop farming it in the traditional way and to let nature take over instead, a process usually called rewilding. I'll explain why we did that and what has happened since, and then we'll walk down to the river.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The honest answer to why is money. The soil here is heavy clay, which makes it very difficult and expensive to farm. For years, we were losing money on almost every crop, and my father was close to selling the land. A friend suggested we look at what had been done on a similar estate in the Netherlands, and that gave us the idea.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So what did we actually do? First, we stopped ploughing and stopped using fertilisers and pesticides. We took down most of the internal fences, so the land became one large area rather than a lot of separate fields. And we introduced a small number of grazing animals: old breeds of cattle and pigs, as well as ponies and deer. These animals act as a substitute for the large wild herbivores that once lived in Britain. As they graze, browse and dig, they create a mixture of habitats: open grassland in some places, thick scrub in others, and young trees growing up through the thorny bushes.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: One thing that surprised us was how important scrub turned out to be. Most people see thorny bushes as untidy, a sign that land has been neglected. But scrub is actually one of the richest habitats for wildlife. It shelters nesting birds, provides food for insects, and protects young oak trees from being eaten by deer until they're big enough to survive.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The results have been remarkable. We've recorded a large increase in the number of species of butterflies and moths, and populations of several birds that are declining elsewhere in the country have grown here. The most famous example is the nightingale. When we started, we had perhaps two or three pairs. Now we have more than thirty, which makes Hartwell one of the most important sites for nightingales in the country.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Three years ago, with permission from the government, we released a family of beavers into the river. Beavers build dams, which slow down the flow of water. That has created a series of ponds and wetlands, which are fantastic for insects, frogs and fish. It has also helped to reduce flooding in the village downstream, because the water is held back and released more slowly after heavy rain.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, how does the estate make money if we're not farming? Mainly through what we call nature-based tourism. We have a campsite, a few safari tents and some holiday cottages, and we run guided walks like this one. We also sell meat from the cattle and pigs, which is in high demand because the animals live outdoors all year. And recently, we've begun to receive payments for storing carbon in our soils and trees, which may become a more important source of income in the future.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Not everyone has welcomed what we've done. Some of our farming neighbours were worried that weeds from our land would spread into their fields, and a few felt that we were wasting good farmland when the country needs to produce food. We take those concerns seriously. We cut back plants along our borders, and we've shared what we've learned with other farmers, several of whom are now rewilding small areas of their own land, such as field edges and riverbanks.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, before we set off, a couple of requests. Please keep to the paths, and keep dogs on leads, because the cattle have young calves at the moment and may be protective. And if you're lucky enough to hear a nightingale, please stay quiet and don't use recordings to try to attract it, as that can disturb nesting birds.

listeningParts.title: A presentation on urban foxes
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two zoology students, Ellie and Raj, prepare a presentation on foxes living in cities with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, you two have chosen urban foxes for your presentation. Why foxes?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Partly because they're so visible. Almost everyone in the city has a story about seeing a fox in their garden or on the street at night. But when we started reading, we realised how little most people actually know about them, and how many myths there are.

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: And it's a good example of a wild animal adapting to a completely human environment, which links to the theme of the module.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. What's the history? When did foxes start living in cities?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: In Britain, it seems to have started in the 1930s, when lots of new suburbs were built with large gardens. Foxes moved in from the surrounding countryside, and the gardens gave them shelter and plenty of food.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: A lot of people assume foxes came into cities because they couldn't find food in the countryside, but there's no real evidence for that. They simply found that suburbs were a very good habitat.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What do urban foxes actually eat? People often say they live mainly on rubbish.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: That's one of the myths we want to address. Studies that analysed what foxes eat found that food deliberately put out by people, for foxes, birds or pets, makes up a much larger part of their diet than food taken from bins. They also eat a lot of earthworms, insects and fruit, and they catch some rats and mice.

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: And one study estimated that about one household in ten in some cities feeds foxes on purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Interesting. How have researchers studied their movements?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Mostly with GPS collars, which record the fox's position every few minutes. The results show that urban foxes have much smaller territories than rural ones, because food is so concentrated. In the countryside a fox might need several square kilometres, but in a city it might be less than half a square kilometre.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: And there's a really nice citizen science project where people put camera traps in their gardens. They've collected thousands of video clips of foxes, and they've shown how foxes use fences and walls as routes, almost like roads.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are foxes active during the day as well?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Mostly at night, especially in busy areas, because that's when there are fewer people and less traffic. But in quiet parks and gardens, they're often seen during the day too, particularly in spring when they have cubs to feed. Traffic is actually the biggest cause of death for urban foxes.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What about the idea that urban foxes are becoming different from rural foxes?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: There's a study comparing skulls that found urban foxes have slightly shorter, wider snouts than rural ones. The researchers suggested this might be because they don't need to catch fast-moving prey so much, and they eat more food that needs crushing rather than tearing.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: But we want to be careful there. It's one study, and the differences are small. We don't want to suggest that foxes are evolving into a new species.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that's a sensible caution. Now, how are you going to structure the presentation?

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with a short video clip from the camera traps, to get people's attention. Then the history, then diet, then movement, and finally the question of conflict with people.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: What do you mean by conflict?

dialogue.speaker: Raj
dialogue.text: Things like foxes digging in gardens, or making noise at night. Some people want them removed. But research suggests that killing urban foxes doesn't work, because other foxes quickly move into the empty territory.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point to end on. I'd suggest finishing with some practical advice on living alongside foxes, rather than just the problem. And keep your slides simple; one main idea per slide.

dialogue.speaker: Ellie
dialogue.text: Okay. We'll have a practice run on Friday.

listeningParts.title: The hidden life of trees
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a plant biology course on how trees interact with each other and with fungi.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's topic has attracted a great deal of public attention in the last few years: the idea that trees communicate and cooperate with each other through underground networks. You may have heard the phrase 'wood wide web'. I want to explain what we know, what is still debated, and why it matters for how we manage forests.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with the basics. If you dig into the soil of almost any forest, you'll find that tree roots are surrounded by extremely fine threads. These are the threads of fungi, and the partnership between the fungus and the plant root is called a mycorrhiza, from the Greek words for fungus and root. Around ninety per cent of land plants form these partnerships.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The relationship benefits both sides. The fungal threads are much thinner than roots and can spread far further through the soil, so they're very good at absorbing water and nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, which they pass to the tree. In return, the tree supplies the fungus with sugars that it produces by photosynthesis. In some forests, trees may give up as much as a third of the sugar they produce to their fungal partners. That tells you how valuable the relationship must be.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, here's where it gets interesting. A single fungus can connect to the roots of several trees at once, and a single tree can be connected to many fungi. So the trees in a forest can be linked together in a network. In the 1990s, the Canadian forest ecologist Suzanne Simard carried out a famous experiment in which she covered young trees with bags and supplied them with carbon dioxide containing a special form of carbon that can be traced. She then found that some of this carbon turned up in neighbouring trees of a different species. This suggested that carbon was moving from tree to tree through the fungal network.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Later studies claimed to show even more remarkable things. One finding was that the largest, oldest trees, sometimes called 'mother trees', are connected to many young trees and may send them carbon, particularly when the young trees are growing in deep shade. Other experiments suggested that when a tree is attacked by insects, chemical signals may travel through the network and prompt neighbouring trees to increase their defences.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: These ideas have been enormously popular. They've appeared in best-selling books and documentaries, often with the message that forests are cooperative communities, a bit like families. However, I need to stress that in recent years a number of scientists have raised serious doubts. A review published in 2023 examined the evidence and concluded that many of the most widely repeated claims are not well supported. The networks certainly exist, but it's much less clear how often carbon is actually transferred in meaningful amounts, and whether this happens because trees are helping each other or simply because the fungi move resources around to suit their own needs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In other words, the fungi are not neutral cables. They're living organisms with their own interests. Some researchers argue that it may be more accurate to think of the fungi as traders, exchanging nutrients for sugar wherever they get the best deal, rather than as a communication system that trees use to cooperate.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever the outcome of this debate, the research has had practical consequences. It has shown that the soil beneath a forest is a vital part of the ecosystem. When forests are clear-felled, meaning all the trees in an area are cut down at once, the fungal networks can be badly damaged, and young trees planted afterwards may grow more slowly. Some forest managers now leave groups of older trees standing when they harvest timber, in the hope that this will help the forest recover. Next time, we'll look at the role of forests in the global carbon cycle.

readingPassages.title: The return of the wolf
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the grey wolf was absent from Yellowstone National Park in the United States. Wolves had been deliberately exterminated across most of the country by the 1920s, hunted, trapped and poisoned because they killed livestock and were widely regarded as dangerous pests. In Yellowstone, even park rangers took part in the campaign, and the last known wolves in the park were killed in 1926. At the time, few people questioned this policy, and some biologists even supported it, believing that an ecosystem without predators would be richer and more stable. Removing large predators was seen as a way of protecting the elk, deer and other grazing animals that visitors came to see.

Over the following decades, however, scientists began to notice changes in the park's ecosystem. Without wolves, the elk population grew dramatically, and the animals spent long periods grazing in river valleys, where they ate young willow, aspen and cottonwood trees before they had a chance to grow. As these trees disappeared from riverbanks, other species that depended on them declined. Beavers, which need willow for food and for building dams, became extremely rare, and the loss of beaver dams changed the way rivers flowed. Some songbirds that nest in riverside trees also declined, and the banks of some streams began to erode more quickly without tree roots to hold the soil in place.

In 1995 and 1996, after years of public debate and legal challenges, thirty-one wolves captured in Canada were released into Yellowstone. The reintroduction was strongly opposed by many ranchers in the surrounding states, who feared that wolves would leave the park and attack their cattle and sheep. To address these concerns, a conservation organisation set up a fund to compensate ranchers for any livestock killed by wolves, and the government allowed wolves that repeatedly attacked livestock outside the park to be shot.

The wolves thrived, helped by an abundant supply of prey. Within a decade, their numbers in the park had risen to more than a hundred, divided among a dozen or so packs. The most obvious effect was on the elk, whose population fell considerably over the following years. But researchers soon began to report changes that went far beyond the direct effect of wolves killing elk. In some river valleys, willow and aspen began to grow again. Beaver colonies increased from one to nine within about a decade, and their dams created ponds that provided habitats for fish, amphibians and birds.

To explain these changes, some ecologists proposed what they called the 'landscape of fear'. According to this idea, elk changed their behaviour in response to the presence of wolves, avoiding open valleys and riverbanks where they could easily be trapped, and spending less time in any one place. This reduced grazing pressure on young trees in those areas, allowing them to recover. The effects of a predator thus spread through the whole food chain, a process ecologists call a trophic cascade.

The Yellowstone story became famous around the world, helped by a popular online video claiming that wolves had literally 'changed the course of rivers'. In recent years, however, many scientists have argued that the story has been oversimplified. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting outside the park, harsh winters and the growing number of other predators, such as bears and cougars. Some studies have found that elk do not avoid areas used by wolves as much as the 'landscape of fear' theory suggests. And in many valleys, willows have not recovered, possibly because without beaver dams, the water table has fallen too far for young trees to establish themselves.

None of this means that the reintroduction of wolves was unimportant. Most researchers agree that wolves have had significant effects on Yellowstone's ecosystem. But the case shows how difficult it can be to separate the effects of a single species from the many other factors that shape an ecosystem, and why it is risky to assume that restoring one missing animal will automatically restore a landscape to its previous state. Nevertheless, the Yellowstone experience has inspired similar projects elsewhere, including the return of wolves to parts of Europe, where their numbers have increased significantly in recent decades.

readingPassages.title: Saving the world's seeds
paragraphs: Deep inside a mountain on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, about a thousand kilometres from the North Pole, lies one of the most unusual storage facilities in the world. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008, holds more than a million samples of seeds from almost every country on Earth, representing thousands of varieties of crops such as wheat, rice, maize, beans and barley. The vault is sometimes described in the media as a 'doomsday vault', but its managers prefer to stress its everyday role. Its purpose is to act as a backup for the world's food supply: if seeds held in other collections are lost through war, natural disaster or simple mismanagement, copies stored in Svalbard can be used to replace them.

The location was chosen for several reasons, after a long search. Spitsbergen is remote and politically stable, and the vault is cut more than a hundred metres into the rock, well above sea level, so that it would remain dry even if the polar ice caps melted completely. The surrounding rock is permanently frozen, which means that even if the electricity supply failed, the seeds would remain below freezing. In normal operation, the vault is cooled to minus eighteen degrees Celsius, a temperature at which many seeds can remain alive for decades or even centuries.

The vault does not own the seeds it holds. It works rather like a safe-deposit box in a bank: the institutions that send seeds, usually national gene banks, retain ownership, and only they can withdraw them. Sending seeds to Svalbard costs them nothing, as the facility is funded by the Norwegian government and an international trust. Each deposit is sealed in a box which is not opened by the vault's staff. The vault is opened only a few times a year, when new deposits arrive, and it has no permanent staff on site; it is monitored remotely from the Norwegian mainland. Countries and organisations of all sizes use it, from large international research centres to small community seed banks run by groups of farmers.

Why is such a facility needed? Over the last century, the genetic diversity of the crops we depend on has declined dramatically. Farmers once grew a huge variety of local types, each adapted to particular soils, climates and uses. As agriculture has industrialised, many of these have been replaced by a small number of high-yielding modern varieties. Although these produce more food and are easier to harvest by machine, relying on them is risky, because a single disease or pest can affect an entire crop. Traditional varieties often carry genes for resistance to disease, drought or heat that plant breeders may need in the future, particularly as the climate changes.

The value of the vault was demonstrated in 2015, when it received its first withdrawal. An important gene bank near Aleppo in Syria, which held seeds of crops adapted to dry conditions, had been forced to stop working because of the civil war in the country. Its scientists, who had relocated to Lebanon and Morocco, requested the return of samples they had deposited in Svalbard, and used them to rebuild their collection. They later sent new copies back to the vault.

The vault has not been free of problems. In 2016, unusually high temperatures caused permafrost near the entrance to melt, and water flowed into the access tunnel. Although no seeds were damaged and the water never reached the storage rooms, the incident drew attention to the potential effects of climate change on the Arctic, which is warming faster than most of the planet. The Norwegian government subsequently spent millions on improvements, including a new waterproof access tunnel.

Some experts warn that a single global vault, however secure, is not a complete solution. Seeds in storage are frozen in time; they do not continue to evolve in response to changing conditions, as crops in farmers' fields do. For this reason, many conservationists argue that it is equally important to support farmers who continue to grow traditional varieties in their own fields, so that these crops can keep adapting to new pests and climates. Seed vaults and living farms, they suggest, should be seen as complementary rather than as alternatives.

readingPassages.title: Should we put a price on nature?
paragraphs: In 1997, a team of ecologists and economists led by Robert Costanza published a paper in the journal Nature that attempted something that had never been done before: to estimate the economic value of all the services that nature provides to humanity. These 'ecosystem services' included the pollination of crops by insects, the purification of water by wetlands, the protection of coasts by coral reefs and mangroves, and the regulation of the climate by forests and oceans. The researchers concluded that these services were worth, on average, around thirty-three trillion dollars a year, considerably more than the total value of the global economy at the time.

The paper provoked fierce debate. Some critics argued that the figure was meaningless, since without these services there would be no human economy at all; in that sense, nature's value is infinite. Others questioned the methods used, pointing out that the calculations relied on combining many different local studies and assuming their results could be applied across the globe. Yet the study was enormously influential. It helped to establish the idea that the destruction of nature is not only an environmental problem but an economic one, and that decisions which appear profitable may actually make society poorer if the loss of ecosystem services is taken into account.

Supporters of valuing nature argue that it corrects a basic flaw in the way economic decisions are made. When a forest is cleared for farmland, the value of the timber and the crops is recorded in national accounts, but the loss of the forest's role in storing carbon, preventing floods and supporting wildlife is not. Because nature's services are usually free, they are easily ignored. Putting a monetary value on them, supporters say, ensures that they are given proper weight. In my view, there is real force in this argument, particularly when decisions are being made by governments and businesses that think mainly in financial terms.

There are well-known examples of the approach influencing policy. In the 1990s, New York City faced a choice about how to protect the quality of its drinking water, which comes largely from the Catskill Mountains north of the city. Building a water treatment plant would have cost an estimated six to eight billion dollars, plus large running costs. Instead, the city chose to spend around one and a half billion dollars buying land and paying farmers and landowners in the catchment area to protect forests and reduce pollution, relying on the natural landscape to filter the water. The decision was presented as a sound financial investment rather than merely an act of conservation.

Critics, however, raise several objections. One is practical: many of nature's benefits are extremely difficult to measure, and different methods can produce wildly different values. How, for example, should one value the existence of a species that has no direct use to humans? A second objection is ethical. Some philosophers and environmentalists argue that treating nature as a collection of services to be bought and sold reduces it to a commodity, and that some things have value in themselves, regardless of their usefulness. If a wetland is worth protecting only because it is profitable to do so, then the case for protection disappears whenever destroying it becomes more profitable.

A further concern is that putting a price on nature may change people's motivations in unexpected ways. Psychologists have found that offering payment for an activity that people previously did for moral reasons can sometimes reduce their willingness to do it. There is a risk, critics argue, that paying landowners to protect nature could weaken the sense that conservation is a duty, so that people come to expect payment for doing what they would previously have done anyway.

These objections are serious, but I do not think they are decisive. Valuing nature need not mean that only financial value counts; it can simply be a way of making visible some of the costs that are otherwise ignored. The most sensible approach is probably to use economic valuation as one tool among several, alongside legal protection for important habitats and recognition of the cultural and spiritual value that many communities place on the natural world. What matters is not whether we put a price on nature, but whether the decisions we make reflect the full range of what we stand to lose.
